newsitem.title: UK: Disputed N.Ireland parade set for Saturday - Mayor.
newsitem.headline: Disputed N.Ireland parade set for Saturday - Mayor.

text.p: The mayor of Londonderry vowed on Wednesday to take part in a disputed Protestant march on Saturday despite fears it might inflame sectarian tension.

Richard Dallas said he hoped to be in an Apprentice Boys parade around the walls of Northern Ireland's second city which was rerouted in August when sectarian violence swept the province because of Protestant marches.
Police said they were considering a request by the Apprentice Boys group to hold their postponed march along the walls, which overlook the Roman Catholic, Irish nationalist Bogisde area of the city.

Dallas, a member of the pro-British Ulster Unionist party, said he was confident the march would be permitted and doubted whether its organisers would hold talks with Bogside residents who want to discuss the route.
"I think it would be very difficult for the residents to meet with the Apprentice Boys for the simple reason that there is a lot of mistrust on the Boys' side," he said.

The march has raised fears among community leaders of inflaming sectarian passions days after the Irish Republican Army killed one soldier in a bomb attack on Britain's army headquarters in Lisburn, south of Belfast.

John Hume, the Londonderry-based leader of the Irish nationalist Social Democratic and Labour party, said he was confident talks could be arranged between Bogside residents and the march's organisers to defuse any tension.
"I would hope that we would be able to resolve the matter to the satisfaction of all sides," said Hume, who mediated in August when the planned parade was rerouted.

Bogside residents objected to the route of the August 10 march which celebrates a 17th Century incident when trainee workers closed the gates of the city on an invading Catholic monarch, King James ll.

The parade coincided with a wave of sectarian violence sparked by a police U-turn on a ban on a Protestant Orange Order parade passing through a predominantly Catholic section of the southern town of Portadown.
Army and police sealed off the city walls with concrete blocks and galvanised fencing to prevent any attempt by the Apprentice Boys to march along the walls.
The Apprentice Boys order said at the time that it would carry out its annual parade at a more suitable time and spokesmen said this weekend had been judged the right moment.
Bogside residents say the march is triumphalists and intimidatory and does not help ease tension between majority Protestants and minority Catholics.
